The legal status of virtual currencies differs from country to country and is still not defined in many countries. While some countries have allowed their use and trade, others have restricted or [[1]] them. There are good reasons why they don’t circulate universally. For one thing, these currencies receive [[2]], including lack of stability in their price, high and dynamic transaction costs, poor security and fraud at exchanges, etc. Apart from these problems, mining virtual currencies requires an enormous amount of electricity, [[3]] a large carbon footprint, which sparks off greenhouse gas emissions.
For another, virtual currencies, such as Bitcoin, are not reliant on any central authority like a government or bank. [[4]], they are designed to function as a means of exchange via computer networks. When a virtual currency is created prior to its issuance, it is generally considered decentralized. Implemented with decentralized control, these currencies utilize the blockchain technology to serve as a public financial transaction database. In this way, virtual currencies can be seen as a form of revolutionary innovation, as they [[5]] and function independently of traditional central authorities. In a word, the legality and impacts of virtual currencies are still controversial around the world.
